analysis.one_liner: Bans shrimp imports from countries whose fishing harms endangered sea turtles.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban shrimp imports from countries that don't protect sea turtles died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Endangered Species Act to make it illegal to import shrimp from any country whose shrimp fleets do not use turtle excluder devices — trap doors in fishing nets that let captured sea turtles escape — or whose activities harm sea turtles' survival. The Secretary of Commerce would publish and regularly update a list of offending nations, and violators would face civil and criminal penalties. Because U.S. shrimp boats were already required to use these devices, the ban would also shield American shrimpers from shrimp caught abroad without the same rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Endangered and threatened sea turtles, which drown in shrimp trawl nets by the thousands when turtle excluder devices are not used. U.S. shrimp fishermen also benefit: the bill applies the same turtle-protection standard they must already meet to every country selling shrimp into the U.S. market, removing a price disadvantage against foreign fleets that fish without the devices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sea turtles and U.S. shrimp fishermen

how_it_helps.text: Cuts off the U.S. market for shrimp caught anywhere by vessels that do not use turtle excluder devices, devices approved by the National Marine Fisheries Service that let sea turtles escape shrimp nets, directly reducing sea turtle deaths.

Goes beyond fishing gear: it also bars imports from nations that allow sea turtle eggs to be taken on their beaches or that engage in other activities that hurt sea turtles' ability to survive or reproduce.
Levels the playing field for U.S. shrimpers, who were already required to use the same turtle-excluder devices on their own vessels, by applying that standard to competing imports.

Backs the ban with real teeth: the Secretary of Commerce must publish and periodically update a list of non-complying nations, and violations carry both civil and criminal penalties under the Endangered Species Act.

analysis.who_pays: Shrimp-exporting countries whose fleets fish without turtle protection would lose access to the U.S. market unless their governments adopted turtle excluder devices or stopped harming sea turtles. Seafood importers would bear the cost of screening sources, and U.S. consumers would likely pay somewhat more for shrimp as cheaper imports from non-complying nations were cut off.

drawbacks.text: The bill's catch-all clause banning imports from nations engaged in 'other activities' that adversely affect sea turtles is extremely broad. Almost every shrimp-exporting country could be listed for nearly any reason, giving the executive branch sweeping, discretionary power over trade in a major food import.
The cost lands partly on U.S. grocery shoppers: restricting imports of a staple seafood typically raises its price, and the bill offers no relief for low-income consumers.

Putting the United States in the position of certifying other nations' domestic environmental practices invites trade disputes with shrimp-exporting countries and hands the Commerce and State Departments a continuous enforcement burden — the two agencies had already been asked to comment on the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation case was real: sea turtles are endangered, U.S. boats already had to use turtle excluder devices, and the bill simply extended that standard to imports. But the bill was drafted loosely — the vague 'other activities' clause could have been used to ban imports from nearly any shrimp-exporting nation at the executive's discretion, and consumers would bear some of the cost in higher shrimp prices. It was a legitimate idea with a poorly bounded design, and it never got far enough for anyone to fix either problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House subcommittee from October 1989 until the Congress ended in January 1991 and never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative James A. Hayes of Louisiana introduced the bill on October 11, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries.
Six days later the committee requested comment from the Commerce and State Departments and sent the bill to its Subcommittee on Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation and the Environment.
Twenty representatives — 15 Democrats and 5 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors, but no further action was ever taken.
The bill died there when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, having never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shrimp-exporting countries kept unrestricted access to the U.S. market with no turtle-protection requirements, and seafood importers kept selling shrimp caught without them; sea turtles gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: James A. Hayes
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban shrimp imports from nations whose practices harm sea turtles.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 17, 1989 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; the furthest it moved was the subcommittee referral.

against.name: Walter B. Jones
against.role: Chairman, House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of referral during a Congress in which the bill never received a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 15 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but the bill never got a vote, so the chamber's partisan split on it was never recorded.

industries.note: These fleets harvest shrimp in turtle-populated waters without turtle excluder devices and would be banned from the U.S. market under the bill. Their cheap, turtle-killing shrimp is exactly what the import prohibition targets.

American shrimpers already must use federally approved turtle excluder devices, so imports from fleets without that requirement undercut them. The bill applies their own standard to foreign competitors, aligning their business interest with turtle conservation.
Importers would have to verify the fishing practices of every source country or drop non-complying suppliers. Their cost-saving access to turtle-unfriendly shrimp would end.
Consumers might pay more for shrimp as non-complying imports are cut off, in exchange for sea turtle protection and a domestic fleet competing on equal rules.
